articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress struggles to find a message that resonates with voters ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Marshall McLuhan's "the medium is the message" frames a midterms fight where both parties struggle to sell voters on affordability and AI policy.
articles.body: Canadian sociologist Marshall McLuhan famously declared that "the medium is the message." But what if the message is just "medium?" Or, perhaps in today’s vernacular, "mid." Both sides are trying to curate what they say to voters to coax them to vote for their party in November. "The message matters," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said on Fox. "We have accomplished a ton. No taxes on overtime. No taxes on tips. We raised the childcare tax credit. The list goes on and on." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE VANCE'S INTIMATE CAPITOL HILL HUDDLE AS REPUBLICANS CONFRONT TOUGH MIDTERM TERRAIN Those are all vestiges of the "big, beautiful bill," which the Republican-led Congress passed last summer. Now Republicans are scrambling to remind voters what they did. "It was a great message last year, and we missed the opportunity, in my view, to talk about the good things we did last year," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., conceded. But Cramer says voters want to know what you’ve done for them lately. And that’s where the GOP could struggle. "People's rearview mirror is getting shorter and shorter all the time," said Cramer. "What you are going to do for me today is more important to them than what you tried to do a year ago." That’s why some Republicans are frank about their prospects at the polls. "This midterm is going to be a f---ing bloodbath," fumed Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who is retiring. "I think that both parties know everyone's putting blame on the Republicans right now." Democrats are campaigning on affordability. The cost of groceries and fuel are top of mind. "What's most important to Americans are pocketbook issues," said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. "And they see the tariff strategy as punishing our allies and punishing their pocketbooks for no purpose." But Democrats are also stumping on a promise. "The top priority in these next two years is going to be holding Donald Trump accountable," said Colorado Democratic House nominee Melat Kiros. "We'll hold this administration accountable for its corruption," House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., warned. "We will subpoena them if we need to," declared Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. It’s unclear if threats of presidential probes could dilute the Democrats’ directive this fall. "When you talk about (investigations)," yours truly asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., "Does that step on your message in any way about costs?" "No, because there's a cost to the American people around corruption," answered Jeffries. "Which is why the American people are demanding that action be taken and that we hold the crooks accountable." FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Still, one Democrat says the party is better politically if it sticks to bread and butter issues. "There are a lot of corruption questions," said Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt. "But I think the gold ring, the brass ring, is focusing on affordability." While Republicans try to remind voters about the "big, beautiful bill," another prominent GOP senator says his party lacks a coherent message. "We're lucky because the Democrats don't have a plan either," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. "Here's the strategy for both sides. ‘The other guys are worse than me.’" So, some Republicans are reverting to a wedge issue that worked for them at the ballot box two years ago. "We're going to tell the story about the closed border. I mean, President Trump has the most secure border in our history," argued Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala. But both parties are evaluating a late-emerging issue: artificial intelligence. "In the next 30 days, as we go into this election, Democrats have an opportunity to basically put AI on the ballot," Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said on MS NOW. Jeffries suggested Republicans are dismissing immediate concerns about AI agents going rogue. "This is a serious thing. It requires urgent congressional action and Republicans are abandoning their responsibility," said Jeffries. "Democrats will not do that." Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, faces a competitive race this fall in the Buckeye State. He tried to blend a sliver of concerns over AI with the "affordability" question last week. The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3. The bill defrays the high utility costs consumers are sometimes forced to pay if they live near data centers. The legislation diverts those bills to Big Tech firms that run the data centers. So, Husted made the case to protect consumers from shelling out extra cash. "If you create the cost, you should pay the cost," said Husted. OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA But Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the top Democrat on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, stood in the way. "It’s not enough for us to tell states to consider making data centers pay for grid updates rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states," said Heinrich. "Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth." The New Mexico Democrat then objected, blocking Husted’s entreaty on the spot. However, Republicans actually think the move by Heinrich could boost Husted, help Republicans and backfire on Democrats. In other words, a Democratic blockade might assist the GOP make the point that they’re for affordability and the other party is standing in the way. Especially on a bill that passed with such overwhelming support in the House. "Now there's a differentiation between Republicans and Democrats. Republicans are looking out for ratepayers. Democrats are not," said Cramer. Fox is told it’s possible the Senate could try again on the data center-related measure before senators leave the Capitol for the midterms. Another on-the-spot, unanimous consent request would take a matter of minutes to either pass or block the bill (again). But a customary debate accompanied by multiple procedural votes likely consumes a week — even if there’s support for the plan. That said, some lawmakers from both sides wouldn’t mind a roll call vote where they’re documented as supporting the issue. Or a vote where Republicans dare Democrats to go on the record opposing it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What that means is that the Senate likely leaves town for the midterms without addressing "affordability." Republicans can blame Democrats — a little. Specifically on the Ratepayer Protection Act. But Democrats aren’t in the majority. They can upbraid Republicans for not addressing some of those pocket book concerns. That’s the "message" ahead of November. As Kennedy suggested, it might fall flat on both sides. Or, as is sometimes said these days, "mid." After all, it is the midterms.

articles.title: Spanberger's data center plan on collision course with her party's green energy push, critics warn
articles.summary: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's data center plan restricts natural gas generation while demanding grid reliability, raising questions about the gap.
articles.body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's data center plan is facing criticism that one of its key provisions may work against itself. Limits on on-site natural gas generation could make it harder, not easier, for large data centers to support Virginia's already-stressed electric grid. The stakes are high because Virginia is already struggling to keep up with rapidly growing data center electricity demand, especially in Northern Virginia, where demand is outpacing the expansion of transmission lines and substations. Restricting on-site natural gas generation could make it harder for large data centers to add dependable power at a time when the state is trying to stabilize the grid while also shifting toward cleaner energy sources. WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE "Everyone recognizes the need for changes in how Virginia engages with data centers. But the governor’s proposal is internally contradictory and raises serious questions about whether it can actually work," Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore told Fox News Digital. Spanberger’s Data Center Accountability Framework calls for data centers to help stabilize the electric grid while limiting the amount of electricity they can generate from on-site natural gas. Kilgore, R-Gate City, noted that the plan states data centers should source their "own clean power" while at the same time seeking to "limit the amount of electricity data centers can generate from … natural gas." The plan also calls for accelerated clean energy development and prioritizes grid access for data centers that invest in "clean energy" or "further limit on-site natural gas generation." "And if they fail to meet the governor’s preferred energy standards, they could face higher taxes," Kilgore said. "What reliable, dispatchable source of power is supposed to fill the gap? That’s not a political question: it’s how the grid works." A Spanberger spokesperson told Fox News Digital the governor's plan is the "most comprehensive and wide-ranging" in the country and that it aims to protect both Virginia residents and the commonwealth's "natural beauty." "The governor’s plan also ends secrecy around data centers by banning non-disclosure agreements and strengthening local approval," the spokesperson said. "While Gov. Spanberger is pushing to hold data centers accountable — an action polling shows is overwhelmingly supported by Democrats and Republicans — the Trump administration has continued to dismiss the very real concerns Virginians have about data centers’ energy, water and land usage." Spanberger’s plan can still allow data centers to construct on-site power because the framework only restricts the use of that power. She also signed a bill by Del. Rip Sullivan, D-Great Falls, that sharply increased Virginia's goals for energy storage, including a target of 1,600 megawatts of storage capacity at homes and businesses. TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT Republicans said they found some common ground with Spanberger on the issue, citing public unease about the explosion in data center construction and stress on resources. "I am glad the governor is finally talking about high power bills and data centers. Virginians already are," Senate Minority Leader Ryan McDougle, R-Hanover, said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. "This should not be a partisan issue." But he also echoed Kilgore’s concern about the plan’s energy-generation dynamics amid looming zero-emissions requirements. "Virginians — Democrats, Republicans and Independents — will tell you the same thing. Their power bills went up. The laws raising electric bills — the tax on carbon, the Virginia Clean Economy Act, solar mandates, and more — should be repealed, and the companies building data centers should pay their own costs," McDougle said. At the same time, some top Democrats criticized their governor’s plan. "The governor is finally feeling the heat but still ignoring the fire," Senate President Pro-Tem L. Louise Lucas told Richmond’s ABC affiliate. Lucas, Portsmouth, said the framework wrongly ignored the need to end tax exemptions for the centers. The debate comes as Virginia is already in the midst of a state-mandated transition away from carbon-emitting electricity generation under the Virginia Clean Economy Act. Under the law, the state’s major utilities generally must retire their remaining in-state generating units that emit carbon by burning fuel by the end of 2045. The law also allows utilities to seek relief from those requirements if compliance would threaten the reliability or security of electric service. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Spanberger’s new framework would push qualifying data centers further in that direction, limiting on-site natural gas generation while prioritizing grid access for facilities that invest in clean energy, reduce backup generator emissions and further restrict their reliance on natural gas. Kilgore’s argument raised new tension. Restricting one source of on-site power before sufficient dependable alternatives are available could create the very reliability challenge Spanberger’s framework says it is intended to prevent. The issue is particularly acute in Northern Virginia, where data center electricity demand is growing faster than the transmission lines and substations needed to serve it can be expanded, according to Loudoun County. In Northern Virginia’s so-called data center alley, officials are already troubleshooting how to stabilize the grid as an explosion in data center construction puts massive sites among densely populated subdivisions. There, Loudoun County leaders say the typical data center requires a continuous supply of 30 to 200 megawatts, enough to otherwise power 200,000 average homes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The county’s explanation of data center development considerations also specifically lists "natural gas reciprocating engines" as one of the avenues for on-site power, appearing to contradict the push by the governor away from the fuel source. Fox News Digital reached out to Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., for additional comment on the matter because he represents the county in Congress and has been a leading voice in the data center debate. Earlier this month, Subramanyam introduced the National Data Center Plan, which would similarly require data centers to pay for their own energy, analyze their effects on the community, environment and national security before beginning construction. The debate leaves the central dispute over Spanberger’s data center plan unresolved on whether clean generation, battery storage and flexible demand can provide enough dependable power to accommodate Virginia’s rapidly growing data center load as the state simultaneously restricts on-site natural gas generation.

articles.title: Dem AG running for higher office dodges questions on bid to free man who killed pregnant woman
articles.summary: Nevada AG and governor candidate, Aaron Ford, ducked questions about his decision to back early release for a man who killed a pregnant woman while out on bond for a series of other violent crimes.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Nevada's Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford is refusing to explain why he personally backed a clemency bid for a convicted killer who took the life of a pregnant woman while out on bail for a series of armed robbery attacks on Vegas tourists, dodging questions on camera as he campaigns to be the state's next governor. State records in Nevada show Ford was listed as the sole sponsor for Norman Smith’s commutation application at a Sept. 16 Nevada Board of Pardons Commissioners meeting. Smith was serving time for killing a pregnant woman in a convenience store parking lot—a crime committed while he was out on bail for a series of armed robbery attempts committed against Vegas Strip tourists, according to court documents and local reporting at the time. Despite Ford's backing, the board ultimately denied the clemency bid, while Ford skipped the commutation hearing that was scheduled and later walked away from a questioner asking him to justify the decision to sponsor Smith's application at a Las Vegas airport. Ford's sponsorship of the convicted killer's early release bid comes as he mounts a gubernatorial run against Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who has repeatedly attacked the attorney general's record on public safety and criminal justice reform. WHITE HOUSE DENIES TRUMP INFLUENCED BY 'PARDON BROKERS' AFTER '60 MINUTES' INVESTIGATION When confronted about the sponsorship, Ford's campaign told Fox News Digital the attorney general missed the hearing due to an out-of-state family medical emergency and argued that sponsoring an application is merely a routine procedural step allowing the Board of Pardons to decide on a specific clemency request—but the campaign repeatedly refused to explain why Ford chose to elevate Smith's specific case. "Are you Aaron Ford?" a conservative tracker asked the gubernatorial candidate as he deplaned in Las Vegas after flying to Arizona, the same day as Smith's Sept. 16 commutation hearing. "I am," Ford replied to the tracker, who went on to tell the Nevada Attorney General that she has been "following his stuff" on social media. "Nice to meet you." The tracker continued with small talk until pivoting to a question about the decision to sponsor Smith's clemency bid. "I have a question, are you—you're sponsoring Norman Smith's pardon, right?" BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW "Uhh, don't know which one you're talking about, but anyway—good to see you," Ford responded before shuffling away with his wife following their trip to visit their college-aged son who was said to be sick. Fox News Digital pressed Ford's team on what his son was facing in terms of an ailment but was not provided an answer. "Is there a reason why you're pardoning him?" Ford was asked as he attempted to skirt away from the questioner. "Good to see you," was Ford's response before walking away. "Take care." "No reason?" the tracker doubled down. CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM Under Nevada Board of Pardons Commissioners rules, an inmate’s clemency application sits in a queue until one of the board’s nine members—which includes the governor, attorney general, and state Supreme Court justices—chooses to officially sponsor it. By sponsoring Smith’s application, Ford elevated the case out of the administrative queue and onto the official state agenda for a full hearing and vote. Based on a Fox News Digital review of official meeting agendas from 2026, Smith’s application was the only commutation request sponsored by Ford all year. In 2015, Smith was free on bail and facing 14 charges in connection with a series of armed robbery attacks on Vegas Strip tourists when he shot and killed the pregnant woman, Tineshea Adams, according to court documents and reporting at the time from the Las Vegas Review-Journal. Court documents show Smith, who was initially charged with murder but was eventually convicted of voluntary manslaughter and three counts of armed robbery, claimed the killing was the result of self-defense. Smith is currently serving a 10-to-39-year prison sentence. Republican political strategist Matt Gorman slammed Ford's silent airport exit, telling Fox News Digital that the attorney general's refusal to answer speaks volumes. "If Nevada's top law enforcement officer can't even explain why he backed early release for a man who killed a pregnant woman while out on bail for a series of other violent crimes, he has no business asking voters to make him governor."

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: In deep blue Minnesota a red dawn may be rising ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: Minnesota's GOP candidates Michele Tafoya and Lisa Demuth are closing in on Democratic Party rivals as a billion-dollar fraud scandal fuels outrage.
articles.body: Six months ago, very few people imagined that this year’s senate and governor races in Minnesota would be anything but Democratic Party blowouts, but as we approach October, and the beating heart of the midterms, the Gopher state appears suddenly and stunningly in play. Recent polling, as shoddy as this cycle’s surveys have been, show GOP senate candidate Michele Tafoya within 2 or 3 points of her opponent, sitting Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, and while the chaos surrounding the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of CBP is in the rearview mirror, the massive Somali fraud scandal decidedly is not. On Sunday, I headed over to Cowboys Saloon in Lexington, Minn., just north of the Twin Cities, to attend a Vikings game watch party for local Republican volunteers, where I found Lisa Demuth, Speaker of the Minnesota House and candidate for governor, rallying the troops ahead of some door knocking and leafleting. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN Demuth is running against sitting senator Amy Klobuchar for governor as the Minnesota Democrats play a high stakes game of political musical chairs, in which poor Gov. Tim Walz has already lost his seat. "We have heard from Minnesotans across the state," Demuth told Fox News Digital, "when we’ve been traveling, that they are ready for a change, it's nice to see the polling start to reflect that, but we were hearing voters ready for a change, ending fraud, making the state affordable, just all the desperate change we have needed." Over the next several weeks, the key question will be whether Minnesota Republicans, and fed-up independents, really believe they can win this time, after decades of Democrat dominance Minnesota’s GOP House Majority Leader, Harry Niska, was also on hand for the 9-3 Vikings victory and offered this explanation to the tightening races: "It’s not a surprise to those of us who have spent months talking to voters in Minnesota as more and more Minnesotans become aware of the billions of dollars that have been stolen from our taxpayers." 'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS The fraud that Niska refers to is, of course, the ongoing scandal surrounding the Minneapolis community in the Cedar Riverside neighborhood, that has been bilking tax dollars with fake learning centers and autism care, to the tune of a possible $9 billion, with a "B," dollars. Indeed, the scandal, now long since a national story, was on the tongues of almost everyone I spoke to, of both parties, in the warm afterglow of the Vikings "W" once the canvassers had left to knock upon doors. MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM "It’s infuriating," Tony, in his late 30s, told me, going on to say, "There’s just no rules, and we all pay for it, it's like, how does this even happen?" I met Bill and Laura, who appeared to be longtime friends over a cigarette and they had two distinct takes on the races. Bill told me of Michele Tafoya, "She doesn’t impress me," then suggested, "I just don’t see the makings for an office for [her]." WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT' But, when I asked how Minnesotans were feeling about their leadership on the state and federal level, it was Laura, without a beat who insisted, "We’re all very discouraged," prompting Bill to admit that Walz, "Took the opportunity to make choices that were not well conceived." In one dire last comment, Laura shook her head and said, "People are losing hope, man." My longest conversation of the day was with Dan, a smart, well-traveled and worldly man with a lovely little dog named Jasper. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Dan is a Democrat who freely acknowledges that bad mistakes have been made by Democrats in his state, but who sees the GOP as an existential threat, "They want to destroy the country," he told me, "just start with data centers, they just seem to serve these corporations." Dan is skeptical that Tafoya and Demuth can pull of the upsets, and gave me one pretty compelling reason why when he pointed a table of about 8 people, various ages, in their purple and gold and finery, saying, "I promise you every person at that table is a Republican, how many do you think will vote?" "Three," I replied, "Maybe four?" To which he simply said, "Bingo." The flipside to Dan’s turnout argument were the two or three dozen volunteers stomping the suburb for the GOP even as we spoke, and having that kind of ground game as early as September is typically something you see from Democrats, not from Republicans. articles.title: Republican senator calls for investigation of Donald Trump Jr., Hunter Biden
articles.summary: Curtis wants an investigation into the alleged personal use of political ties.
articles.body:
Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis is calling on Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and Ranking Member Dick Dubin, D-Ill., to subpoena both Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden as part of an investigation into "the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit, preferential treatment or access by domestic and foreign interests" that Curtis is urging the senators to open.

Curtis' letter comes after he posted a video on X Friday saying that reports that Donald Trump Jr.'s two-day wedding afterparty in May had been funded by a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin "stink" and are "corruption." He promised further action on the topic.

President Donald Trump said last week that his son had repaid the oligarch for the afterparty costs, though no evidence of that alleged repayment has been publicly offered.

"As I understand it, he paid them back. He didn't want to have that, so I hear he paid them back. A person that he knows pretty, I guess a friend of his, gave him a wedding party. That's very common," the president said .

"The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president. Nor should congressional oversight begin and end when control of the White House changes hands," Curtis writes in the letter .

"I therefore respectfully request that the Senate Judiciary Committee launch an investigation into the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access by domestic and foreign interests," Curtis' letter continued. "As part of that investigation, I urge the Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to testify regarding their past business dealings, relationships with foreign individuals and entities, gifts, or other benefits they have received, and any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value."

Hunter Biden, the youngest son of former President Joe Biden, has faced years of Republican and congressional scrutiny over unproven claims that he and his father, who was then vice president, allegedly pressured a Ukrainian oligarch to pay them millions of dollars to orchestrate the firing of a Ukrainian prosecutor who at the time was investigating Burisma, the energy company of which the oligarch was CEO. Hunter Biden sat on Burisma's board at the time.

Sen. Durbin said Tuesday that he supports Curtis' "good faith request" for the investigation.

"Corruption must never be tolerated," Durbin said in a statement , in part. "To ignore this is to run the risk of being complicit. I will join in supporting Senator Curtis' request of the Judiciary Committee."

When asked about Curtis' request on Capitol Hill Tuesday afternoon, Sen. Grassley told ABC News he couldn't comment because he hadn't yet read the letter.

Curtis is not a member of the Judiciary Committee and would not be involved in any vote to subpoena Hunter Biden or Donald Trump Jr. However, his is the most direct admonishment regarding recent reports concerning Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding that has come from any Republican on Capitol Hill.

In his letter, Curtis raises direct concerns both about Hunter Biden's "substantial business with foreign entities ... while his father held or sought public office" and about "the relationship of President Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., with foreign business figures and the acceptance of significant gifts."

Curtis writes that concerns about Trump Jr.'s activities are "compounded" by his "promotion of family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, his continued pursuit of international real estate deals involving direct meetings with foreign heads of state, and his reported investments in defense contracting."

"These reports raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president's family and whether such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment," Curtis writes. "They also may create expectations of a returned favor that would not be in the best interests of the American people or our allies, and could even create national security vulnerabilities."

articles.title: From campus radicals to Beijing's AI sabotage: Rep Randy Fine says 'US fighting to save Western civilization'
articles.summary: Florida Congressman Randy Fine on being an unapologetic defender of the MAGA agenda and the pressing need to emerge victorious against China in AI battle
articles.body: U.S. Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., has emerged as one of the most outspoken foreign policy voices in Congress during his short tenure on Capitol Hill. He frames the modern political battleground not just merely as a domestic election but as an existential struggle to preserve Western civilization. In a wide-ranging exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the Florida Republican pulled no punches as he tied anti-Israel sentiment and opposition to domestic AI data centers directly to foreign influence operations by Iran and China, positioning himself as an unapologetic fighter for President Donald Trump’s agenda. GOP REP RANDY FINE DECLARES THAT DEPORTING ALL ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IS THE TOP WAY TO MAKE THE US AFFORDABLE As the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has emerged as a political lightning rod, serving as a primary litmus test for the American left, Fine believes foreign money has played a large part in shaping public opinion. "I think it's a focused effort over many decades to try to pollute our population with these ridiculous ideas," Fine said. "But I think it's accelerated since Oct. 7 as massive amounts of foreign money have come in to try and manipulate public opinion through social media. They lie. And here's how you know they lie. When other countries kill tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of their people, no one seems to be bothered. "But when Israel defends itself from a terrorist attack, they lose their minds. Iran killed 40,000 of its own people in a couple of days earlier this year. Those same people who are upset with Israel are actually siding with Iran. The good news is the vast majority of the American people understand that the United States and Israel are fighting to save Western civilization, and that's certainly a message that I'm focused on spreading every day." As the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is sweeping through mainstream culture with the recent cancellation of Macklemore's tour dates in football stadiums, Fine is a staunch defender of Robert Kraft's decision and denies it's merely "conservative cancel culture." "So, first off, they weren't political statements," Fine said. "I mean, is calling for the death of Jews a political statement? I mean it's antisemitism in the same way racism against black people is. And while you're allowed to be an idiot, as this Macklemore guy is, you don't have the right to perform in a stadium that's owned by private citizens. "He didn't want a guy who puts a prosthetic nose on his face, in order to appear to be a Nazi, performing in his stadium. He has every right to say that is not welcome. "That doesn't mean Macklemore can't stand on the street corner and preach his views. Cancel culture is when you cannot exist, when you're debanked, when you literally cannot function in society. "But in the same way, I have the right to say whatever I want, other people have the right to you can't say it in my house. And that's all that's happened here. I think he [Robert Kraft] did the right thing. I think we need more of it." AOC JOINS MACKLEMORE FUNDRAISING MEMO TARGETING ROBERT KRAFT Fine has also been at the forefront of condemning the militant pro-Palestinian protesters who have taken over university campuses across the country over the past year. "I think we draw the line at violence. Every student has the right to get an education," Fine said. "And, so, for example, when Jewish students are not able to come to class, when they're not able to walk across campus, when they're blamed for the actions of a country on the other side of the world, that is where you've crossed a line. "Look, I had to deal with the ‘free Palestine’ idiots when I was in college, you know, 30 years ago. But they didn't affect my ability to actually exist and to do my job and to be a student. So. I just didn't worry about it." Fine has described himself as "MAGA through and through" and sees himself as one of the president's staunchest defenders in Congress. "Well, I believe in making America great again. I've been a huge supporter of the president," Fine said. "I was the first member of the Florida House to support President Trump when he ran for president again in 2024. And I believe that the president is really putting his fingers in the dam of the destruction of Western civilization, which so many are trying to shove down our throats. "So, I'm here to be a warrior and a soldier for President Trump's agenda, and I've been proud to do it since I got elected on April 1 of last year." As domestic opposition to data centers has skyrocketed and AI regulation emerges as a major issue heading into the midterms, Fine warns that China is using both issues to win a geopolitical advantage over the United States. "I think it's largely an op by China. And let's explain why. So, I think the 21st century, who wins the 21st century, will largely be defined by who wins the war over AI. And that fight is on four levels. "One is hardware. Who has the best hardware? Right now, America is in the lead on that. Who has the best software? Right now, America is on the lead. "Who has the best energy infrastructure? Unfortunately, China has the lead on that because while the idiots on our side have said let's not have coal-fired power plants … let's not have nuclear, let's get all of our energy from solar and windmills, China, who's selling us all the solar and the windmills, is putting up coal-fired power plants. So, cheap, plentiful energy. China's winning that fight. "But the fourth front in that fight is what they call compute: data centers. If you want to use Grok, if you want to use ChatGPT, if you want to use Claude and you type that stuff in, something needs to be doing the thinking. It's not happening on your phone. It's happening at a data center. And China has realized that if they can get America to not put data centers in, well then those data centers have to go in China, and China wins on that front of the war. "Does that mean you should be able to put a data center in a neighborhood? No, it doesn't. But does that mean the data centers are a critical part of re-industrializing the United States to make sure we win the war over AI? It absolutely is." Finally, Congressman Fine addressed the looming midterm elections as Republicans face headwinds to retain control of both chambers, making a forceful case for the GOP's accomplishments in the 119th Congress. "Well, I'd say two things. No. 1, look at what we've done. The largest tax cut in American history. No tax on tips, no tax on overtime. Look at President Trump sealing the border. Look at the first net migration out of the country in decades. Look at the stopping of the transgender things. Look at all the extraordinary achievements. Remember how bad things were two years ago? Many of the Democrats that I serve with hate America. If you think Ilhan Omar, if you think Rashida Tlaib, if you think Abdulrahman Mohammed El-Sayed, if you think Zohran Mamdani, if you think they think America is good and that they love America, you're out of your mind. "And the Democratic Party has been poisoned by people who hate America. The barbarians are no longer outside the gates, they're inside and they're running for Congress. And they can never be allowed to have power because they will make it their single-minded mission to destroy the country."

articles.title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in custody case involving newborn with heart condition
articles.summary: The Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect.
articles.body: Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday rejected a request for the Supreme Court to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect. McKenna West gave birth to the couple’s baby in Texas last month and argued in court there that California denied her due process when it awarded custody of the child, whom she named Gabriel, to his genetic parents. A Texas judge dismissed her claims. She then appealed to the Supreme Court. Kagan denied to issue a stay in the case in a Tuesday order with no written decision. In a filing earlier this month, attorneys for West urged Kagan, who handles emergency matters involving California, to intervene because a “life hangs in the balance.” They said West is concerned that Gabriel might not get the medical care he needs if he remains in the custody of his parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar. Gilkar told a judge in Dallas last month that she and her husband were dedicated to getting the son they named Rumi the help he requires — and that the “unstable” West is making an already tragic situation more fraught. “She’s making us run from doctor to doctor, state to state with our baby. She’s trying to take him,” Gilkar testified. The Texas Supreme Court issued a ruling last week allowing the baby to be moved to California, where the parents have medical care for the child lined up, the Texas Tribune reported. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the ruling said. The baby was born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital defect in which one side of the organ is underdeveloped, preventing normal blood flow. The condition can quickly become fatal if it is left untreated. According to court documents obtained last month by The Associated Press, the newborn was in critical condition and “suffering from potential complications” following heart surgery in Texas. The parents had turned to surrogacy after efforts involving in vitro fertilization treatments failed. They signed a contract in August 2025 with West — a cardiac nurse who was living in Anchorage, Alaska — that included a clause stipulating the pregnancy could be terminated if there was a “fetal abnormality.” West said the parents tried to invoke the clause after the heart defect was diagnosed, but she refused to comply. She ultimately headed to Texas, where her case was championed by state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for a U.S. Senate seat this fall. With Paxton’s assistance, West got an order directing that the newborn get necessary lifesaving care in Texas after he was born. The parents had planned for him to get that care in their native California. Judges in Alaska and Texas ultimately deferred to the California ruling, according to West’s Supreme Court filing. West alleges that Ahmed and Gilkar violated their surrogacy agreement by seeking custody in California. She said the agreement had called for any legal challenges to be heard in Alaska. West contended that the California decision should be tossed out because she did not get proper due process, and she said she is being kept in the dark about the baby’s health. In a court filing, West said that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” The parents’ attorney said that they are focused on the baby’s health and that West is engaged in “political theater.”

articles.title: US halts Obamacare enrollment for over 760,000 enrollees, claiming fraud
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is halting enrollment in Obamacare health plans for more than 760,000 enrollees it believes were fra...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is halting enrollment in Obamacare health plans for more than 760,000 enrollees it believes were fraudulently signed up, Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday, part of an ‌anti-fraud effort he estimated would save $2.2 billion in taxpayer money.

The US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services canceled about 315,000 plans last ‌month, citing unverified citizenship or immigration documentation and suspected improper enrollments.

The agency will bar 569 brokers it accused of submitting "statistically implausible rates of plan year 2026 applications" without necessary ​applicant information such as a Social Security number.

The plans, created by Democratic President Barack Obama's signature Affordable Care Act, offer income-based subsidies. Republican President Donald Trump sought unsuccessfully in his first term to overturn the law and has proposed changes that would make the plans less comprehensive.

Millions dropped coverage this year as rising medical costs and the expiration of extra COVID-era subsidies made monthly premiums unaffordable.

Vance described the canceled group as "a mix of both phantom ‌people, but also real people who just don't ⁠meet the eligibility requirements," including some he said who were signed up by brokers without their knowledge.

Vance said the administration would further verify between 419,000 and 450,000 more people to confirm they are legal US residents meeting ⁠income thresholds.

CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said the enrollees were treated as "phantoms" because officials believe most either do not exist or were unaware they had coverage, having never filed a claim and being unreachable despite repeated contact attempts.

The administration is using an emergency-style rulemaking process to impose an immediate, industry-wide freeze ​on new ​Obamacare broker registrations, bypassing the usual advance notice-and-comment period. Oz called it a "temporary ​national moratorium" for six months, saying most fraud was ‌concentrated among such agents.

CMS said some brokers have allegedly enrolled people without genuine consent, changed people's plans without permission, used inaccurate information, or created questionable applications to receive commissions.

The agency said brokers without a 2026 registration will be frozen out until February 1, 2027.

The freeze could weigh on insurers that rely on brokers to sign up customers, analysts said.

Because brokers are key to how people enroll, the freeze "may negatively affect enrollment and potentially margins related to higher risk pool in a market that is already contracting" as enhanced subsidies expire, said Morningstar analyst Julie ‌Utterback.

A blanket moratorium "would punish legitimate professionals instead of targeting the bad actors responsible ​for fraud," said Mychal Walker, president of the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, ​a trade group that urged CMS to adopt targeted safeguards ​instead.

CMS said unauthorized Obamacare enrollments could cost up to $6.6 billion in improper federal spending for the 2026 plan ‌year.

The cancellations were led by Vance's anti-fraud task force, which ​includes Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy ​Jr., Oz and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson.

CMS said it expects a return of about $2.2 billion in advance payments of the premium tax credit for the canceled enrollments. Oz said the figure would climb, calling it "the tip of the iceberg."

An HHS report released ​earlier this year estimated nearly half of new ‌Obamacare enrollments between 2021 and 2024 may have been improper, phantom or fraudulent. CMS said more than 1 million enrollees ​received coverage without providing a Social Security number.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson and Ahmed Aboulenein in Washington, Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; ​Additional reporting by Susan Heavey; Editing by Alexandra Hudson and Bill Berkrot)

articles.title: Trump’s focus on the press distracts Republicans from pocketbook issues ahead of Election Day
articles.summary: The media ban has dominated the news cycle for days, and rather than steer the conversation back to economic issues, has Trump amplified the furor.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Zigzagging from issue to issue, President Donald Trump has left his political allies struggling to keep pace with his pronouncements and lost precious time to drive a compelling message ahead of the midterm congressional elections, Republican strategists and people who’ve worked with him said. The takeaway from recent polling is that voters worry most about high prices and the cost of living. But Trump has at times veered off pocketbook issues and made moves that are peripheral to the top-of-mind concerns of voters who will soon decide which party controls Congress. The latest instance of Trump stepping on his party’s own messaging came on Friday. In the hour before he held an Oval Office event focused on reducing prescription drug prices, Trump announced he was barring three news outlets from the White House grounds because he disliked their coverage. That caught even some members of his own staff off guard. The media ban has dominated the news cycle for days, and rather than steer the conversation back to the savings Americans would reap from his policies, Trump amplified the furor. Some Republican candidates in competitive races are increasingly distancing themselves from the president, believing that voters want a different focus and tack than what Trump is offering. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who is typically a staunch Trump defender, released an ad criticizing Trump’s mass deportation agenda. And GOP candidates in Iowa and Michigan have spoken out against the Iran war and its effect on prices. Nearly two-thirds of adults lack confidence in the national news media, according to an NBC News survey in June sponsored by More Perfect, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to advancing democracy. That makes the press a ripe target, though it isn’t clear that Americans want Trump to do something about it. In an NBC News poll this month, registered voters cited inflation, government corruption, threats to democracy, jobs and the economy, the Iran war, immigration and healthcare costs as issues that loom largest; news coverage was not presented as an option. “The president is out there touting his new arch,” Maura Gillespie, a Republican strategist, said of Trump’s plan to build a soaring arch near Arlington National Cemetery. “None of that addresses the gas prices being over $4. None of that addresses the younger voters who are struggling to afford their first home. None of that is landing.” “Republicans need to steer their messaging away from Trump and divert their lane from him and focus on their constituents, because that’s the only thing that’s going to get them elected,” she added. Trump often complains that news coverage fails to credit him for his successes. Labor and stock markets have proved resilient in Trump’s term, though wages are lagging inflation. “The story no one is writing is how well the economy is doing in spite of the president’s lack of discipline,” said a person close to the administration, who added that Trump, 80, is growing “more impulsive with age.” Speaking at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump spooled out a list of accomplishments on his watch. He struck a triumphal tone as he cast the U.S. as a nation in the midst of a renaissance. “Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on earth. Our technology is second to none and we’re leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet. America is rising, our nation is growing, our power is expanding, our country is doing better than ever before.” A White House spokesman, Kush Desai, said in a statement: “The Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the president’s long-term economic agenda on the home front. Continued private-sector job growth, booming investments, and month-over-month prices of beef, chicken, prescription drugs, and other essentials declining in the last two inflation reports are all proof that America’s positive economic momentum continues.” In recent months, Trump has slalomed back and forth through the issues. In April, he threatened to destroy Iran’s civilization. Hours later, he backed off. He called Iran’s leaders “very rational” in June, “scum” in July. In his United Nations speech, Trump revived his apocalyptic threat. He warned that he may need to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” if the regime doesn’t agree to a deal to end the war. This month he announced that he would send every American a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterm elections; a key Republican senator whose committee oversees spending plans told reporters he had seen no details of how Trump’s idea would work. “He’s very unpredictable. He calls it trusting his gut,” a second Republican senator told NBC News, who, like others in this piece, requested anonymity to speak candidly. The press ban The latest thunderclap from Trump’s social media feed was his eviction of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds. A number of high-level White House aides were unaware beforehand that Trump had imposed the ban, and they struggled to explain it in the hours after it went into effect, according to conversations with four White House officials. Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles was absent from the building Friday when he announced the new directive, according to a person familiar with the situation, potentially leading to some of the confusion from the staff. Still, aides sought to defend Trump’s move. “Nobody close to the president was surprised at his action to hold the fake news accountable,” a senior White House official said. Even Vice President JD Vance seemed at a loss as to how to explain the policy. Trump said specifically that he was “banning” the three outlets. But Vance, speaking to reporters Monday before heading to a campaign stop in North Carolina, said: “So, he’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying, ‘We’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.’” In an interview with the “TODAY” show, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked whether media outlets should be banned because Trump doesn’t like their coverage. Rubio defended the president’s decision, saying, “There aren’t a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it’s called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House.” MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett were all denied access to the White House on Saturday. Klein and Haslett both had their White House press credentials confiscated when they sought to enter the grounds. In his remarks Friday, Trump said, “We are banning them, yes we are, and there may be others to follow.” But a Trump adviser told NBC News on Tuesday “there are not” conversations happening inside the White House about expanding the ban to other disfavored outlets. The TV networks have set up what’s known as a “pool”; they take turns covering the president as he goes about his public activities and sharing footage with other news outlets. CNN was supposed to provide TV pool coverage on Monday, but the White House barred them from their duties. In response, the four other networks that are part of the TV network pool — NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox — refused to step in for the exiled CNN, meaning there was no TV pool coverage. The repercussions were soon evident, potentially impeding Trump’s ability to deliver his message. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, tried to air the president’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony, but he couldn’t be heard. “There’s no microphone because the pool cameras aren’t there. So maybe, Tim, this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” the Newsmax host said, adding, “So obviously, the ramifications are here. Can’t hear what the president is saying.” Trump’s ban is now before a judge. All three outlets filed suit against Trump on Monday, arguing that their eviction violates both due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, set a hearing for Wednesday afternoon on the plaintiff’s motion for a temporary restraining order. Trump has long lamented his media coverage. During his first term, the White House barred a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, from the grounds following a contentious public exchange with Trump. CNN sued and the judge in the case — also Kelly — ordered the Trump administration to return Acosta’s press pass. In the end, the administration relented and restored the pass permanently. In the new term, Trump has also talked privately about barring individual reporters and news outlets from the White House, but he refrained, according to two people familiar with those discussions. By acting now, he may be distracting from a promising message for his party ahead of the midterms. Internal White House polling shows that Trump’s effort to reduce the cost of prescription drugs is his most popular issue, according to a White House official. “He can and should be talking about the things that voters say are really important to them. And this [the media ban] is not it,” said Douglas Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee. “It seems to have come out of nowhere and it seems to have caught a lot of people by surprise.” “We’re less than 45 days out from the election and for the last three days no voter has heard anything about what Donald Trump wants to do to lower prices,” he added. “That’s a problem for any Republican on the ballot.” The second Republican senator rattled off a series of issues that he’d like to see Trump spotlight. “He can go out and talk about the reduction in crime,” the senator said, “or controlling the border, or eliminating rules and regulations.” “But he’s probably not.” ‘Be quiet’ A recent run of setbacks has soured the mood inside the West Wing, a senior White House official said. Even though Trump now has a handpicked chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, the board defied Trump’s wishes last week and raised interest rates. The Supreme Court has blocked Trump’s attempt to use the Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms, something Trump had hoped to do. Gas prices have spiked since the Trump administration and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, creating a slow-rolling backlash within the GOP. Growing numbers of Republicans in tight midterm races are finding ways to distance themselves from Trump, whose approval rating in a new NBC News poll stood at 41%, a second-term low. Rep. Ashley Hinson, an Iowa Republican who faces a tough race for the Senate, called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war in a social media post Monday. That’s an about-face from Hinson, who has voted against resolutions directing Trump to stop the war six different times. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.” On Friday, Trump got some unsolicited advice from an iconic figure in the cultural world. Pat Boone, the 92-year-old singer-songwriter, released a video on X that offered a heartfelt suggestion to the president. “Right now, I feel like you’re very tired,” Boone said, looking straight at the camera. “And I’m worried that many of us haven’t prayed enough for you because I think you’re wearing out and you’re feeling the pressure and expressing yourself in ways that are not becoming to you — that are not presidential.” “So may I recommend something very highly: that you be quiet.”

articles.title: Russia's neighbor reveals personal appeals to Trump as US weighs NATO troop pullback in Europe
articles.summary: Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda revealed he sent two letters to Trump urging U.S. troops to stay on NATO's eastern flank amid Russian threat.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda revealed Monday he personally pleaded with President Donald Trump to maintain U.S. forces on NATO’s eastern flank as Washington reviews its military footprint in Europe. Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine has raged on for more than 4½ years and raised questions about how far Moscow will push into the continent. Nausėda said during remarks at a fireside chat moderated by Fox News Digital at the Presidential Business Forum on Resilience on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly New York that Lithuania is prepared to provide "very generous host nation support" for American forces to remain in the region. "I personally sent two letters to the president," Nausėda said of the plea to keep an American troops' presence. PENTAGON CUTS BRIGADE COMBAT TEAMS IN EUROPE AS TRUMP PRESSURES NATO ON SPENDING The Pentagon has already begun scaling back some forces and capabilities in Europe, while reported options under review could remove tens of thousands more troops. The review is part of a broader Pentagon strategy to shift primary responsibility for Europe’s conventional defense onto European allies, while reserving a more limited U.S. role. But Washington has also signaled that its retrenchment may not be uniform: Trump said last week that the U.S. was making progress toward a permanent Army base in Poland, one of NATO’s highest-spending members. That has left frontline allies trying to determine where they fit in with an emerging U.S. strategy that calls for a smaller overall role in Europe while deepening ties with countries Washington views as carrying more of the burden. The review also comes as Russia’s war with Ukraine has increasingly spilled into NATO territory. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS Lithuania experienced that threat firsthand last week when NATO fighters shot down a drone that crossed into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Nausėda later said the aircraft was likely Russian and intended for an attack on Ukraine before veering off course. The country's intelligence services warn that Russia is already rebuilding military capabilities near NATO's eastern borders despite its losses in Ukraine. Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment found that a ceasefire or frozen conflict in Ukraine could accelerate that buildup, allowing Moscow to move more troops and equipment back toward permanent bases near the Baltic States and replenish weapons and ammunition depleted during the war. In that scenario, Lithuanian intelligence assessed Russia could eventually develop enough capability to launch military action against the Baltics and seek an initial regional advantage before NATO could fully respond. Asked how much time NATO would have if a ceasefire were reached tomorrow, Nausėda declined to put a timeline on the threat but warned that "a ceasefire for Russia may mean" looking for new targets. He said whether Moscow ultimately tests NATO would depend largely on the alliance's ability to strengthen its deterrence and demonstrate that it can defend its eastern flank. Nausėda cast doubt on the prospect of near-term peace talks, saying that "for the time being, Russia is not ready to start the peace negotiations." Instead, he said Moscow appears intent on using the approaching winter to increase pressure on Kyiv by striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and worsening conditions for civilians. "The winter is coming. Russia knows very well where they should target, and they will target energy infrastructure first of all," Nausėda said, describing the attacks as an effort to make living conditions in Ukraine as difficult as possible and pressure its leadership toward concessions. "For these negotiations, I don’t see any ground, at least right now," he said, adding that talks could become possible "maybe next year." The threat to energy infrastructure was particularly resonant for Nausėda, who spoke as Lithuania marked another step in its yearslong effort to insulate itself from energy pressure from Moscow. Lithuania, marking a new long-term natural gas agreement with U.S. natural gas producer EQT Corp. this week during the president's trip to New York, began importing U.S. LNG in 2017 and now gets roughly 70% of its LNG from the United States, Nausėda said. During Monday’s forum, Lithuanian energy company Ignitis signed a new long-term LNG agreement with U.S.-based EQT Corp. Nausėda said Lithuania’s push for energy independence was shaped by years of experience with Moscow using the country’s dependence on Russian energy as political leverage. "Our history shows that, all the time, Russians misused our dependencies for their own benefit," Nausėda said. Nausėda stressed that Lithuania is also increasing its own defense burden, saying the country is spending 5.4% of GDP on defense while building a national division and preparing to host a full German brigade by the end of 2027. articles.title: San Francisco sues Trump Media over alleged 'pay-to-play' Truth Social service
articles.summary: San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu alleges the paid service gives wealthy subscribers an unfair advantage by providing early access to President Donald Trump's market-moving posts.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's social media company is facing a lawsuit from the city of San Francisco over a paid Truth Social subscription service that gives certain customers early access to the president's posts. San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu announced the lawsuit Tuesday, alleging that Trump Media's Truth API service operates as a "pay-to-play scheme," allowing subscribers to receive President Donald Trump's market-moving posts before they are publicly available. The lawsuit seeks to block the service and impose civil penalties under California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL). Chiu alleged the service gives wealthy subscribers an "unfair advantage" by providing early access to government information before it reaches the broader public. TRUMP WARNS HE'LL BE 'LAST REPUBLICAN PRESIDENT' IF SENATE GOP DOESN'T MAKE MAJOR CHANGE "Truth Social has knowingly created a marketplace for insider trading by giving high paying subscribers an unfair advantage over ordinary investors in the market," Chiu said at a Tuesday press conference. "It's a pay-to-play scheme for early access to the president's market-moving government decisions." The monthly subscription was rolled out Aug. 1 and costs between $60,000 to $100,000 in exchange for early access to market-moving posts from Truth Social accounts with large followings, including Trump’s own account. "No ordinary person can pay that fee," Chiu said. "Now the early subscribers are largely high-frequency trading firms with the technology to analyze that information and to make trades within microseconds." TRUMP ANNOUNCES WHITE HOUSE BAN AGAINST THREE MEDIA OUTLETS Chiu also said Trump owns roughly 41% of Trump Media and "is personally benefiting from this business scheme." A Trump Media spokesperson pushed back on the allegations, telling Fox News Digital: "The People of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the left-wing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information." The lawsuit was filed Monday — the same day that dozens of former federal prosecutors and agents filed a court brief backing a separate lawsuit over Truth API, according to CBS News. TRUMP’S $100K WALL STREET TRUTH ACCESS DRAWS LAWSUIT; EXPERT WARNS IT ‘RAISES THE STAKES’ ON ETHICS The separate lawsuit, brought by The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation, alleges the paid service violates the First and Fifth Amendments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A White House spokesperson referred Fox News Digital to Trump Media and The Trump Organization for comment. Representatives for The Trump Organization and Chiu's office could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment. Fox News Digital's Julia Bonavita contributed to this report.
